Paint the Town Red is a medium-paced bar fighting game with a large variety of weapons and enemies now and here to come. It still needs a bit of optimization, but the devs assure us that the game will be optimized as the game progresses (And updates.)

The enemies are completely destructible. You could dissolve someone if you have enough time and the weapon doesn't break. All the voxels on the enemies have different properties, with bone being the strongest natural voxel and skin being the weakest. (You will be able to damage Riot Helmets later on, but those aren't natural.) Additional fact, is that if a enemy's brain is damaged in anyway, they will instantly die, if they don't, its a bug.

The weapons range from messy steaks and urinal cakes, to Katanas and Shotguns. All of them have different durability, damage, throw damage, voxel damage, and maybe even a unique trait, such as being able to instantly stun someone if you hit them in the head area with Soap or a Urinal cake. [url=http://gfycat.com/KindlyAlarmingGrouse]Example of a enemy being stunned in utter disgust with a Urinal cake.[/url] (You do not need to directly aim for the mouth to stun the enemy, and you can stun a enemy with any blunt weapon if you hit them in the face, though it is random.)

The combat is quite intense as it is mostly melee combat, you can do overhead and right side swings and normal attacks. You can also kick of which knockback power and damage depends on how full the bar is. Full means a guaranteed knockdown. (Knockback has not been implemented yet.) Throwing damage, speed and range also depend on the bar level. But if you sit ontop of the bar throwing mugs at people, you aren't playing the game right.

Extending on the Combat subject, if you damage a enemy enough, they will go into a enraged mode dealing extra damage, having extra speed and attack speed.

If you are having problems with FPS, look at the low performance section of the "Common Issues" thread I linked above. Otherwise, the game runs quite well when you select the appropriate options for your machine. (In game options.)

I rate PTTR (Paint the Town Red.) 9/10.

Positives:
-Fun Combat.
-Great Mechanics.
-Active Developers.
-Very Friendly Community.
-Relatively fast updates when they're not working on bigger things. (1-2 Monthly big updates, weekly small updates.)

Small Negatives.
-Still needs a bit of optimization. (The Disco Dancefloor.)
-A bit of bugs, not necessarily gamebreaking, but immersion breaking.
-Rare crashes.

I bought this game because it looked like the FPS equivalent of a giant stressball.  I've been working a lot lately, and sometimes when people are being bull headed, I just want to grab a pool cue and really take my day out on the side of their faces.

Enter "Pain the town red".  There's no story, no character development, no dialogue, just you - disgruntled for whatever reason - I mean, I assume you are, you could be a happy go lucky psychopath - and your fists.

So a guy walks into a bar.

And proceeds to beat and stab the living shit out of everyone there.  He beats the security, the bar and wait staff, the other patrons, walks into the back room and kills the owner, his bodyguards, the guys he was meeting from the other bar down the street. 

The bars are littered with weapons and crap to hit people with.  So there's even an element of exploration as things up high are usually some kind of weapon you've never seen before.

There's also a nice challenge game mode where you fight in an arena.  

This is what indie developement is all about, if you ask me.  Focus on a single gameplay element and explore how it can be a fun, meaningful, interesting game in and of itself.

Definitely recommend.

I'll get my criticisms out of the way:

- The game definitely has performance issues
- Weapon durability is a bit too low
- (In my opinion) enemies shouldn't follow you as tenaciously.  If I accidentally pass near a large group, I end up in a boring cycle of of running, hitting, running, hitting, picking off enemies one by one until the group is small enough to take on directly.  I don't mind that enemies chase you, but maybe have them split off and start fighting each other again after a while.

As for the good:

- Combat is awesome.  Feels very tight and responsive despite being simple.
- Gore effects are great.
- Physics feels satisfying!
- Interesting concept with promise of more maps to come!

Overall I'd totally still recommend the game, and I imagine the kinks will be worked out over the next few updates.

A great sandbox fighter game with a lot of options to play and replay various scenarios and workshop access, allowing for a near infinite supply of content.

The game also has a rogue-like dungeon crawler on top of all the sandbox fun that initially existed, adding what is the value of basically a second game of a different genre, with similar mechanics, on top, for absolutely free (That's what I feel about it, as I bought the game in early access, wayyy before Beneath was even on the table). Beneath is a great dungeon crawler, with many different levels, mechanics and upgrades to take you through the different bosses of the game, most of them with their very own environment and even full levels with new enemies, just to build up to another boss fight.

The game offers sufficient mechanics to fight in a Rogue-like environment, while also giving you sandbox scenarios with neat looking locations and special enemies. The scenarios then have many modifiers to choose from, to alter the way you or the enemy plays, giving great replayability to each scenario. Also  the game has powerups, which you can use and mess with in sandbox, with many abilities exclusive to Beneath, giving you different classes.

If you run out of content when all of these options are exhausted, there is still the arena mode to try and challenge you to beat certain waves with limited resources, and there is the steam workshop accessibility for new scenarios and enemies, handmade by the community.
You can also play many aspects of the game with friends.

(After studying some negative reviews of the game I have to say: I don't care that you can't swing from the left, honestly who cares, I can hit them from the right, good enough for me; also git gud lmao)

Worth full price. Although I'd always recommend waiting for a sale if you're not too amped to play the game, I won't (and can't) be the judge of your spending habits though.

Paint the Town Red is a fine time waster. For Scenarios, at least.

Until you look at it's secondary mode: Beneath.

Beneath is the "Darker and Edgier" mode that actually feels like a game, and the difficulty ramps to very hard. It's a hard Rogue Like, to be exact.

You have [b] 4 classes, [/b] (Brawler, Magic, Speed, and a Jack-of-all-stats, all with different stats and abilities) and run through different underground landscapes (Caves, Crystallized Caverns, Lava Caves, ect) actually fighting off more than just some humans. Zombies with tentacle arms, crystallized crabs with a near OHKO laser beam, floating heads, short skeletons with powerful laser staffs, giant digging worms, 3-headed mini hydras, lightning mages, spiders, and much more.

When you die, you have to [b] restart from the beginning again, [/b] but you can buy [b] permanent upgrades in the middle of your runs, the only things you keep between runs. [/b] (More weapon options to find, more ammo for ranged ones, more stats like health and speed)

Perks are scattered throughout the caves, and are normally bought with gold. (status effects on enemies, knock-back enemies, better attack speed, having a constantly respawning NPC fight on your side, more weapon durability, more speed when out of combat, and more)

There's [b] minor boss fights, [/b] the Shard Lords, all with varying degrees of annoying and difficult. They drop "Shards of a fallen God" [b] which you can spend outside of runs, for much better permanent upgrades. [/b] (more perks, better compass, and upgrading the playable classes)

There is a minor story you have to find out yourself, and you do have a main goal: defeat the main 4 bosses of this mode. Named the Elder Gods, this is when this game's difficulty starts to go really hard. 

[h1] Now that i'm here, i just realized that I spent most of this review talking about how Beneath works, and not my actual opinion. [/h1]

Beneath actually feels like a fairly challenging, complex, and fun game, instead of the simple playground/simulator feel of the main scenarios.

That fixes my main problem with the game. [b] It's no longer lacking in content. [/b] Now there's something to do, and a reason to play for more than 30 minutes.

So either you want a playground of blood, or a complex first person rogue like, this is an interesting option. [b] A very unique option to buy. [/b]

I find Paint The Town Red to be so much fun I actually have questioned a couple times whether this game has brought out some dark, deep-seated psychotic side in me. This is, without a doubt, the most entertaining beat-em'-up I have ever played. The combination of wacky yet semi-realistic physics, pixelated brutality (in impressive detail for a pixelated game), sheer amount of action taking place all around you at once, the amount of ways to beat the absolute sh*t out of people, and some of the most satisfying blows I have ever delivered unto another person, makes this, as I said, the most fun beat-em-up I have ever played. Allow me to, later on, go into more detail on most of these points.

There are only three levels out right now (Bar, Disco, Prison) as well as a sandbox level, as of this review. However, the developers seem committed to this game, and I am insanely jittery to see new maps being released at some point. Imagine a gym/wrestling ring, city block, mansion, fairground, subway...a bit of Gang Beasts comes to mind when thinking of levels that could be added to this game. And, as those new levels come out, hopefully along with even more weapons, character models, etc., I will be pouring WAY more time into this game than my current 9-10 hours shows, as of this review.

The way the blunt weapons, such as the bat or the baton, smack into your enemies' temples, causing copious and comical amounts of blood to spurt continuously from their face, and then having the next hit warranting their entire face to crumble into chunks as their body crumples to the ground(yes, this actually happens sometimes. I'll explain later), delivers, as I stated, some of the most satisfying combat and victories I have ever seen in ANY type of game.

The game isn't very far from the truth at all when it states you can use pretty much anything not nailed down to take out your opponents. Hell, in the prison levels, you can rip off the shower nozzles and use them as a weapon. YOU CAN THROW APPLES AT PEOPLE. I HAVE KILLED PEOPLE WITH APPLES. I HAVE PUT DENTS IN PEOPLE'S FOREHEADS WITH F***ING APPLES. THINK ABOUT THAT.

The amount of action going on around you for most of the fight, as you work to take out every other living being in whatever building you are dropped into, makes for a constant adrenaline rush as you uncontrollably spout profanities at the various enemies tromping towards you, weapons in hand. You are never safe until every last being is taken out, and, very much like in a real fight, you have to always look behind you to make sure someone is actually dead (even with the signature snare sound that plays whenever someone is dead, you still can miss a few people), or to make sure someone hasn't spotted you and started stalking you with their only goal being to cave your head in until they can use it for eating Ramen.

The physics have multiple chances each brawl to showcase their realism and their wackiness, depending on the scenario. Especially with the "hard hitter" match modifier, kicking people with a full "kick" bar (or whateverthef*** it's called) sends them flying across the map, hitting the roof sometimes (not exaggerating) or getting booted up to a higher floor. In other scenarios, the way some of the weapons bounce off the walls, or the way an enemy will crumple to the ground or fall onto their @ss after a particularly hard hit with a bat, will add to the satisfaction of taking someone out in a more realistic fashion.

The gore in this game is certainly something that I did not see coming, at least not to the extent that it turned out to be. This is strangely one of the most violent games I have ever played. I had no idea until I started beating someone's face in with a tire iron the first time that you can literally TAKE APART someone. Their entire bodies are destructible. Every pixel. And each pixel is colored in to resemble flesh, bone, muscle, or brain. To a pretty accurate degree, given the size of the pixels. You can chop off arms at any area, not just joints (I think), same with legs. You can decapitate people (sometimes VERY cleanly, which will leave you saying "OOOOOOHH SHITBISCUITS" or something at least that's what I would say shut up). You can even curb stomp a f***er until his pixelated brain is showing. This game is brutal in the most comical and satisfying of ways.

Allow me to, off the top of my head, list every weapon in this game. As they come to mind. Beer bottle, cup, cleaver, knife, machete, kitana, pool cue, pool ball (cube), toothbrush shiv, basketball, shower nozzle, frying pan, slab of meat (yes, really), soap (YES, REALLY), money ("I am sad that I lack the talent to make this sh*t up" -Jontron), tire iron, bat, dumbbell, barbell, barbell weights (small and heavy), barbell pole, ham (I'm done), lunch tray, apple, orange, various chairs, nunchaku (hidden), shuriken (hidden), lightsaber (only in sandbox level currently), guitar, shotgun (hidden). Not all of these can be found in each level, however, each level is of decent size and packed with weapons. Imagine more levels with MORE weapons to be found depending on what new levels we get.

Now, before I go to my conclusion, I do need to tell that another part of what makes this game so satisfying is that it is surprisingly difficult at times. Like stated before, if you don't watch your back constantly, a couple blows to your head with most weapons will kill you just as easily as the next guy. Not only that but it can be very easy to get surrounded or in a corner if you don't know your surroundings well. Most of what makes this game difficult are reasons that can be attributed to fighting in real life. Not only this, but there are also "boss"-esque characters in each level, that don't come out to attack you right away. For example, the boxer in the bar level basement, who takes a POUNDING and can take you down with 4-5 punches. Even when it comes to a normal dude, though, a few hits with a bottle, a couple slashes with a machete, etc., and you're down and out, and you have to restart. This game has managed to literally make me jump when I forget to watch my back and I turn around to leave a room and there's a big brolic black dude named Requis ready to skullf**k me.

The game is so addicting, though, that you can't really give a lot of a sh*t if you wanted to. Especially since you have the ability to combat this difficulty with magical powers of blowing people up (yes, really). You have a bar in the top left that charges up as you beat the sh*t out of people, and as of this review, there are three powers you can choose from. The first that gets unlocked is "Shockwave", which releases a ring of kaboom-y juice around you that throws enemies back, across the entire room in some cases. It's good for when you get in a tight situation, but it doesn't do much damage. The second power is "Berzerk", which turns the game into slo-mo, and you have the ability to one-shot MOST enemies with your fists, and see their heads/bodies/wherever you hit them explode into a bloody pulp. This helps if you have a lot of guys following you and you need a break. The final ability is "Smite", which allows you to make a gun shape with your hand, point at people, and have some otherwordly power bring holy, explod-y, bloody death to their entire body at the click of the mouse. This is good for taking out bigger enemies as well as just taking out a large group of people. It's great in general.

In conclusion, this game is hilarious, brutal, satisfying, addicting, and a time-waster all rolled into one. It can also be a very good stress-reliever. I cannot recommend Paint The Town Red enough, and I really hope the devs stick to this game for weeks and weeks to come, adding new stuff to it as often as possible. Delicious things could come to this game in the future.

"Paint the Town Red" is a 1st person brawler with simplistic graphics, yes, but that is because almost all enemies in the game are voxel-based.  It started out as just a mindless free-for-all brawling game where the objective was to be the last man standing.  You could use almost anything in the environment as a weapon and as you defeated enemies, you would build power for unleashing super powers like the Shockwave punch, the berserker state where you shatter all who stand before you with single super powerful blows, or the Smite which calls down the power of a giant laser to reduce all to gore.

For those not aware, "voxel-based" refers to something being made up of hundreds or thousands or more tiny shapes designed to be chipped away or specially deformed.  In this case a light punch against a person in this game gives them a black eye, but not by swapping the texture of his face but rather shifting the colors of his facial voxels to a black/purple.  Stab him with a knife and he recieves an actual stab wound as the knife destroys the voxel in the wound area, revealing a fleshy or bony interior.  Yes, this game has gore and it is made up of lil square shapes.

This game has since expanded with pvp and the rogue-like dungeon mode "Beneath".  "Beneath" plays alot different from the main game in that you can start off picking which upgradable class you want to play as, giving you different stats and powers.  Then head down into the caves below and wreck things.  You get three different currencies which can be spent in different ways: gold can be spent on relics, weapons, heals or enchantments.  Shards are spent on permenant unlocks but must be spent within the dungeon.  God Shards are only earned from bosses and can only be spent at a special store in the facility above (after rescuing the shopkeep from the dungeon), giving you more powerful permenant unlocks.  Paths, rooms, enemy placements and challenges are all completely randomized as well as the presence of the "Pursuer"... an indestructible foe capable going through walls to chase you relentlessly.

The Pluses and Minuses:

+++ It is incredibly satisfying the way the game allows you to take your enemies apart in a visceral way.
- Enemies getting back up to chase you when they have no arms and no face and thier chest already opened.
- Enemies do ALOT of damage, so challenge level can be up there.  Hand-to-hand combat without weapons feels discouraged.
+ Nearly anything can be a weapon.
++ Steam Workshop support has a huge base!  There's tons of additional stages that people have made along with new textures, weapons, enemies, etc.
+ Built-in gif capture on the pause menu captures the last several seconds of gameplay, all you need to do is click "post" or "download" to share your favorite moments!

Overall, I love this game.  It's a cartoonish, bloody good romp with tons of depth thanks to the "Beneath" mode.  HIGHLY recommend this game, even at full price!

This game is both too small and too big if that makes sense. It's one part proof of concept that didn't quite work out but with some tough and satisfying challenges, and one part infinite beach where the locals visit to make sand castles of every size and skill level.

What kind of game is this? The experience is of playing the bare-knuckled action hero of a first-person B movie which got rated R for violence, blood and gore. Combat is the kind of chaos where you can disappear into the flow of punching, kicking, and attacking with a large variety of real and makeshift weapons; like breaking a knife off in someone's face, then grabbing a frying pan to finish the job.

The “main game” features 5 official scenarios with decently designed but generic areas (with one getting day and night versions) and your one job is to kill everyone so the level exit will appear. Every scenario is a tense marathon battle without healing or mercy. A small sandbox where you can spawn weapons and enemies with various ongoing effects is a great place to train.

Scenarios also offer a bunch of modifiers, including: lights out and living dead for a zombie apocalypse feel, zero g and hard hitter so your kicks can send enemies bouncing off the ceiling, green mode if you want no blood or splatter mode if you want more, weak enemies for an easier time or weak player for a challenge, various ranged weapon modes with an option for unlimited ammo, slo mo to replace running with slowing time, modes to start with different special abilities and unlimited special power, different combinations of the above … it's just too bad there's only the 5 official scenarios.

There's also the Arena with 5 difficult challenge runs of 7-10 fights in a row – some of which are like neat puzzles – where you heal half your health after each fight. Another option in the Arena is the tough and extremely random Endless mode, but don't try this until you've gone Beneath.

The roguelike Beneath campaign is the late-arriving star of the game, a solid but somewhat basic descent through large procedural generated mazes where you die at the end but your next character might get a bit deeper. There are classes which have different powers and playstyles; the ranged Warlock is probably the easiest long-term, while the speedy Spectre is a lot of fun. Perks found along the way don't feel like they become unique builds, and some feel like they should have been the default, like adding to max health with each kill.

Sadly the story is a bit simple (we dug too deep) and the elder god bosses can be a bit easy – but there's no shame in looking up the method to reach the third. There's also a bunch of new fantasy monsters in the mazes, from basic zombies and cultists to weird mages and demonic beasts. A strangely cute hydra is plain annoying to kill. Overall Beneath is fun and stands on its own as an experience, but doesn't have the polish to be its own full game.

Finally we get to the real source of hours spent in this game, player-made levels. There are tough missions where you storm castles and fight off hordes, maps where you can wander peacefully around small beachside towns or through the wilderness, huge city zones where you can enter some of the buildings to visit businesses and apartments, and tiny little single rooms with 88 enemies and an unbreakable sword.

There are over nine thousand (well over 13K) player-made maps, which of course follow the usual bell curve of some gems, some trash and too many okay maps. Unfortunately a lot of good ones are probably lost in the pile and you could spend a long time combing through. Try collections to find good stuff: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2677284524 This one seems to have quite a few, and there are also videos and lists on the web. Personally I believe the Workshop should have had better tags to sort the levels from the start.

And that's it. That's the whole game: not enough of the good official scenarios and Arena challenges, a basic but addictive roguelike, and many thousands of player-made levels. But the flaw for the game would be its combat and core concepts; the ability to gouge off the voxels that make up enemy bodies is sick as hell yet mainly cosmetic only.

You can strip an enemy's face to the skull below, but if they have health remaining, they can still fight with no problem. Or if you attack their arm, you might break off a limb, but it barely inconveniences them. Legs are more reliable quick-kills, but some enemies are just immune to that. What's the point of breakable voxel bodies if they just have hitpoints?

Also melee attacks feel limited with just a quick thrust, a strong side swipe, and a knockdown kick – especially the swipe, because you can't change the angle to cut downward or diagonally. The game is about turning ordinary items into weapons that break bodies, but I can't call this a martial arts game because attacks are simple and only sometimes precise enough to break enemies as intended.

Melee weapons feel a little weird too because they don't have custom animations. A baseball bat or a tire iron make sense when you power swing them, but feel strange with the quick thrust attack. The spear and pike grant amazing range with the thrust, but don't suffer from close quarters on a big swing other than perhaps hitting someone you didn't intend. A hammer or club always look wrong because they feel like they should have downward swings.

With all that said, this game is still great. If you like extreme action movie violence, like watching a guy whose arm just got cut off stopping to look in horror at his stump, this is the place to experience that in first-person over and over and over again. If you want to cut through a room of disco dancers with a katana and then make a gif of that to share with friends, this is your game. If you want to desensitize yourself to blood, come paint the town red.

Paint the Town Red is easily one of my favorite satisfying games! Every moment spent playing is worth it, with endless fun and chaos. The Steam Workshop community is fantastic, full of talented creators who consistently deliver amazing content. If you're looking for a game with tons of replay value and a creative community behind it, this is a must-play!

Pretty much anything can be picked up and used as a weapon, be it a wine bottle that smashes on impact or a wooden bar stool. Combat itself is pretty simple: hold down your left mouse button to swing the weapon, hold down your right mouse button to block. Kill everyone while trying not the get killed yourself.

The game's greatest strength is its wide variety of different game modes. You can fight through several scenarios, go on a roguelike dungeon crawl, or survive waves at the arena. The game also comes with an easy to use level editor and there's a wealth of player-made scenarios to play through once you're done with the official ones.

Scenarios are hand-designed levels where your goal is to kill everyone and return to the exit. The game's scenarios are: a biker bar, a 70s disco, a prison, a wild west saloon, and a pirate village. Each scenario has different weapons for you to use, tailored to the different settings. In the biker bar you will mostly beat people up with bar stools, in the disco you can pluck combs out of people's massive afros and use them as stabbing implements, and in the pirate village you get to use swords! Each scenario starts out peacefully with everyone just going about their business, until you throw the first punch. Then, an all-out brawl breaks out and people start fighting each other. It's very chaotic and very fun.

All of the game's scenarios can also have various modifiers applied to them. There's one that adds guns to the level (which are a lot of fun to use), another makes enemy heads more squishy so they explore more easily... and the latest moddifier added as an April Fool's joke replaces the blood texture with flowers, for those hippies who want to make love, not war.

While I generally prefer hand-made levels of randomized ones, the roguelike mode is the one I spent the most time on because of how huge it is. You start out in a cave and have to descent further and further, fighting your way through hordes of zombies (who are very squishy and often explode in satisfying fountains of gore), human enemies, and various monsters. You can pick up various weapons on your way through the dungeon, but each weapon has a durability and will break down after a while, forcing you to always scavenge for new weapons. If you like action roguelikes, this mode alone makes the game worth buying.

And then there's the arena mode, which I consider to be the weakest. You are dropped into an arena and have to face several waves of enemies. These waves are hand-designed, not random, and are intended as a challenge. Sometimes you will face a horde of armed enemies while you don't get a weapon, forcing you to fight them with your fists until you manage to take one down and steal his weapon. Some of these fights are pretty unfair and more frustrating than fun to attempt.

And finally, there's the level editor... I played through dozens of community-made levels and some of them are even better than the original scenarios. Good stuff. The modding community is in good health and keeps releasing new levels, so the game keeps receiving more and more content for you to play. Another game that proves how valuable mod support is.

With the amount of different game modes and the great mod support this game provides, I can wholeheartedly recommend it. It's good fun, and it gives you so much value for your money it's not even funny.

The man on the end of the bar is looking at you funny.
A Japanese crimelord wants you dead.
You've been incarcerated, even after you've pleaded not guilty. 
It was self-defense, after all.

Let's paint the town red.

Paint the Town Red is, in a nutshell, a beat 'em up from a first person perspective. It's you and your blocky fists against many other blocky men in an orgy of blood and violence. Voxel violence.

Blows landed will bruise, cut, break, and dismember your enemies, spilling their square blood onto whatever surface is nearby. Anything and everything is a weapon. Bar stools, steak, bottles, afro combs, shuriken, bats, pimp canes... really, the list goes on. Nothing will stand in your way once you unleash your god-like special powers. Stack enough bodies and unleash shockwaves, pop men like balloons using nothing but your fists, and finally, call down the wrath of God and literally smite your enemies, reducing men into lifeless piles of wasted carbon.

The three levels available as of this writing are fun and colorful, bursting with personality and secrets, and they include:
-A biker bar where everyone wants to take a bite out of you
-A Saturday-night beatdown at the local disco
-A maximum security prison where dropping the soap is the least of your worries
There's even a sandbox level to play around with or to learn the finer points of Paint the Town Red.

Do I recommend this? Absolutely. Great for blowing off steam, laughing with the fun physics, or even feeling like the 90's action movie hero you always wanted to be.

What can I say about this game that my playtime doesn't already say. I want to give this a fair review but I should say that this is a game that I cannot recommend enough, even for a couple of hours of smashing heads. 

The content: PTTR started with some scenarios and some basic features and a map creator, and since then the scope of content added has been immense. The game has scenarios to get you started, it has a sandbox mode, it has a massive catalogue of user made levels some of which are genuinely beyond impressive and play better than the scenarios do. An arena challenge mode for veterans to test their skill, and a full story mode that takes the form of a roguelike RPG which is impressive enough to be it's own standalone game and what a good chunk of my hours are represented by. This game has almost infinite content and you can play for hundreds of hours and not get bored. 

The gameplay: The gameplay is also an incredibly strong element of this game, it takes the form of a brawler, the controls are simple enough to be considered intuitive to new players but also have a remarkable of mechanical depth and let you bludgeon, stab and dismember people in countless macabre and creative ways. The game has a vast array of weapons from a tape dispenser to a claymore to a fully automatic rifle. The game really let's the playr loose in an environment to create as much chaos as possible and the voxel physics add a feeling of further chaos to the game as people will literally explode into pieces. The game also has powers you can utilise as kill streaks that only enhance the carnage creating experiance. 

The map maker: I have never once used it as my passion lies in the work of almighty Khorne. However, I can say with absolute certainty that it seems incredibly detailed as some of the maps I have seen people make really defy expectations. Perhaps the best aspect of the map maker is the ability to share custom assets on the workshop or use them for yourself which means you won't be having to make skins and items from scratch. Maybe not to everyone's interest but certainly worth a look if you have that creative passion to make in game levels. 

Beneath: Beneath is a Roguelike mode that deserves it's own section really. It has all the hallmarks of a roguelike RPG, wide variety of monters and mobs, different classes, weapons, playstyles, and the ability to play co-op with others. Beneath is really it's own game that uses the vehicle of PTTR to create an incredibly enjoyable, addictive and satisfying experience. Anyone who likes games like Hades should definitely give this a try, its absolutely fantastic. 

Conclusion, this game is a masterpiece made by these devs who have prioritised player freedom, variety and gameplay while still giving the game it's own unique graphical charm. If you are on the fence about this one or you've just found it and somehow slogged through this review, I cannot recommend it enough. It's a minimal investment for a massive amount of content and the devs should be proud of what they have achieved here and the price makes it feel like it's stealing for what you are getting out of it.
